Simply put, WAV (Waveform Audio File Format) is better for recording and editing because it is uncompressed and lossless, while MP3 (MPEG-1 Audio Layer III) is better for sharing and streaming as the files are much smaller. Choose WAV when audio quality matters most, and choose MP3 when file size and compatibility matter more.

WAV is an uncompressed, lossless audio format. MP3 is a compressed, lossy audio format that removes audio detail to make the file smaller.

WAV and MP3 are two of the most common file formats for audio projects, but they both have advantages and disadvantages. Before you hit export on your project, it helps to know where each audio file format shines. In this guide, we’ll compare WAV vs. MP3 files to help you choose the right format for your next audio project.

## Summary

• WAV and MP3 are two popular file formats for digital audio recordings.

• WAV files are not compressed, which means they maintain the original audio quality.

• MP3 files are compressed, making them easier to store and share. But compression means they lose some of the quality from the original recording.

• In general, WAV files are best for recording and editing, while MP3 files are better for casual streaming and sharing.

## WAV vs MP3: The differences at a glance

Here’s an overview of the key differences between WAV and MP3 files.

Uncompressed and lossless, preserves all original audio data

Compressed and lossy, removes audio data to save space

Highest possible audio quality and fidelity

Very good, but small details may be missing

Professional audio recording and editing, audio archives

Casual audio streaming and sharing

## How the WAV format and the MP3 file format work

Both WAV and MP3 are file formats used for sharing audio recordings, but they work differently. The biggest difference between the two is lossless vs. lossy audio.

A WAV file preserves the raw waveform from the original audio recording without removing any data. As it isn’t compressed, the audio’s details are still present with no losses. Due to that, WAV offers the best possible audio fidelity in a digital file.

An MP3 file, on the other hand, compresses the audio recording to make the file smaller. It does this by using psychoacoustic compression to remove audio details that listeners are unlikely to hear or notice. While the overall audio quality is still very good, MP3 doesn’t provide the same audio fidelity and detail that WAV does.

MP3 files can also range in quality depending on their bitrate. 320 kbps is the highest-quality bitrate for MP3s, providing very clear audio. Bitrates of 96 kbps or less are noticeably lower-quality.

When creating an MP3 file, you can also choose between constant and variable bitrate. Constant bitrate files keep the audio quality the same across the entire recording. Variable bitrate files adjust the bitrate throughout the recording based on the complexity of the data, which delivers better audio quality for a given file size.

In short, WAV keeps all the audio data, while MP3 trades some detail for a much smaller file.

## WAV vs. MP3 file size, sound quality, and compatibility

When selecting an audio file type for your projects, there are a few key factors to consider: file size, sound quality and fidelity, and compatibility with your workflows and audience.

## File size

WAV files are much larger than MP3 files. One minute of CD-quality stereo audio (44.1 kHz, 16-bit) takes up about 10.6 MB as a WAV file, compared with about 0.96 MB as a 128 kbps MP3 and about 2.4 MB as a 320 kbps MP3. That makes a WAV file roughly 11 times larger than a 128 kbps MP3 and about 4.4 times larger than a 320 kbps MP3. If you’re creating audio content at scale, you could quickly run out of storage space using WAV files.

WAV files are also more difficult to share because of their large size. They take much longer to upload and download than MP3s. Some email and messaging platforms also limit the sizes of attachment files, making them difficult to share through these platforms.

## Sound quality

WAV files have higher audio quality than MP3 files. As stated above, this is because they preserve the entire audio recording without removing any data, while MP3 files are compressed.

That said, MP3 files still offer good audio quality, especially if they have a higher bitrate. For most casual listeners, the difference between an MP3 file and a WAV file is minimal.

## Compatibility

Another key factor to consider is file compatibility with your devices and the devices your audience is using. This is especially important if you’re exporting a project for a specific use case, like producing podcast audio to upload to a supported platform.

MP3 files are compatible with virtually any device or software that streams audio, including smartphone apps, desktop web browsers, and stereo systems.

WAV files are compatible with most modern devices and software platforms. However, some platforms may struggle to process a WAV’s large size efficiently. Some older stereo systems and streaming platforms do not support WAV files at all.

If you plan on distributing a podcast or music file to a wide audience, an MP3 file is a more accessible option.

## When to choose WAV for recording, editing, and production

WAV files are best for scenarios where audio quality and fidelity are your top priorities, and you have enough digital storage available for large audio files.

When you’re recording and editing an audio project, it’s best to use WAV files to preserve audio quality. With a WAV file, you’ll be able to hear all the details in the audio as you’re editing to help you make informed creative decisions.

If you edit with MP3 files, the audio will be compressed every time you save a new version or make a copy. Over time, this compression adds up, which affects the quality of the final product. Using WAV files through the editing process prevents this problem.
